A voltage tells us something about energy, but voltage and energy aren't the
same quantity.
Electric potential is potential energy per unit charge in a specified source
field.
One volt means one joule per coulomb.
Potential difference between two points gives the energy change per unit
charge
as we move between them.
For a charge q, change in potential energy equals q times final potential
minus
initial potential.
The work done by the electrostatic field is the negative of this energy
change.
An external agent moving the charge without changing its kinetic energy does
work equal to the potential energy change, assuming no other energy transfers.
Let's move a positive two microcoulomb charge from thirty volts to ten volts.
Potential difference is minus twenty volts, so potential energy decreases by
forty microjoules.
The field does positive forty microjoules of work.
If the charge moves freely with only electrostatic force acting, that can
become a forty microjoule increase in kinetic energy.
Now replace it with a negative two microcoulomb charge.
Same endpoints, but potential energy increases by forty microjoules.
The sign of charge matters.
Electrostatic force is conservative, so field work depends on
the endpoints rather than the path connecting them.
Choosing a different zero of potential changes absolute values, not potential
differences or physical work.
Begin each problem by writing final minus initial before inserting numbers.
For a localized point source charge, choosing potential zero at infinity gives
potential k Q divided by distance r.
Keep the sign of Q.
A positive source gives positive potential, and a negative source gives
negative potential with this reference.
Unlike electric field, potential is a scalar.
With several stationary sources, calculate each signed potential and add.
Suppose plus two nanocoulombs and minus one nanocoulomb are each twenty
centimeters from our observation point.
Using k equal to nine times ten to the ninth, their potentials are plus ninety
and minus forty five volts.
Total potential is forty five volts.

At their midpoint the potentials cancel to zero, while their fields point in

So zero potential does not prove zero field.
For an electric dipole far away compared with its separation, potential is
approximately k times dipole moment times cosine of the angle to the dipole

On its equatorial plane, potential is zero with infinity as the reference, but
the field generally is not.
Close to either dipole charge, use the two individual point charge potentials

Scalar addition is simpler than vector addition, but it doesn't remove the

How does a potential map tell us the field?
The field points toward decreasing potential.
In one dimension, the x component of field is minus the derivative of
potential
with respect to x.
More generally, potential difference is minus the line integral of field dot

The minus sign is essential: moving along the field lowers potential.
Imagine potential in volts given by one hundred minus twenty times x, with x
measured in meters.
Its slope is minus twenty volts per meter, so the field is plus twenty newtons
per coulomb along x.
The one hundred volt constant shifts the reference but does not affect the
field.
In a uniform field of three hundred newtons per coulomb pointing right, moving
twenty centimeters right changes potential by minus sixty volts.
Moving the same distance left changes it by plus sixty volts.
If a negative two microcoulomb charge moves right between those points, its
potential energy increases by one hundred and twenty microjoules.
It is moving against its electric force, even though it moves along the field
direction.
A positive charge would lose potential energy for the same displacement.
On a graph, use the slope of potential to find field; don't divide potential
by

For motion perpendicular to a uniform field, the dot product is zero, so
potential does not change.
That gives us the idea of an equipotential surface.
An equipotential surface collects points having the same potential.
Moving a charge along it produces zero work by the electrostatic field,
because
potential difference is zero.
That does not mean no force acts, or that any possible external agent must do
zero work.
It specifically states the electrostatic work between these endpoints.
Where the field is nonzero, it must be perpendicular to a smooth equipotential
surface; a tangential field component would change potential along the
surface.
Around a single point charge, equipotentials are concentric spheres.
Closer spacing for the same potential steps indicates a larger field
magnitude.
A connected conductor in electrostatic equilibrium has constant potential
throughout its material and on its surface.
Constant does not mean zero.
Consider an isolated conducting sphere of radius ten centimeters carrying one
nanocoulomb.
With potential zero at infinity and no external sources, its surface potential
is ninety volts.
Its interior potential is also ninety volts, even though field inside the
material is zero.
At twenty centimeters from its center, potential is forty five volts.
The outside relation is k Q over r, while the inside value stays at k Q over
the sphere radius.
Don't extend the outside one over r expression all the way to the center.
The interior field is zero because the potential has zero spatial slope there,
not because the potential value itself must vanish.
Now distinguish potential at a point from the interaction energy of a whole
charge system.
For two point charges, with zero interaction energy at infinite separation,
energy equals k times their signed charge product divided by separation.
Like charges have positive interaction energy; opposite charges have negative
interaction energy.
Plus two microcoulombs and minus three microcoulombs separated by thirty
centimeters have interaction energy minus zero point one eight joules.
Separating them quasistatically to infinity requires positive zero point one
eight joules of external work, with no change in kinetic energy.
For three charges, add the interaction energy of each distinct pair: one with
two, one with three, and two with three.
Counting every pair twice is a common trap.
This is interaction energy, not the self energy of ideal point charges.
Finally, a fixed electric dipole in a uniform external field has orientation
energy minus p E cosine theta, with zero chosen at a right angle.
Parallel alignment gives the lowest energy and is stable; opposite alignment
gives the highest and is unstable.
Take p equal to two times ten to the minus eleven coulomb meters and E equal
to
one hundred thousand newtons per coulomb.
Rotating quasistatically from parallel to opposite alignment increases energy
by four microjoules.
The external agent supplies that much work.
Always state which energy you're calculating, the reference you chose and
whether the charge distribution or field is being held fixed.
